extracted.intended_audience: readers/students of political philosophy and moral/epistemic theory (early-modern educated audience)
extracted.subtask_description: Normative and classificatory guidance (from Hobbes' Leviathan) on intellectual virtues, defects (madness), kinds of knowledge and sciences, and social concepts of power, worth, dignity, and honour. The page supplies definitions, distinctions, examples, and behavioural signs used to evaluate minds and social status.

rubrics_metrics.name: Virtue defined as eminence by comparison
rubrics_metrics.description: Vertue generally ... is somewhat that is valued for eminence; and consisteth in comparison.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Virtue is not absolute but comparative: if all things were equally in all men nothing would be prized. The value of a quality depends on being distinguished relative to others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intellectual virtues (good wit)
rubrics_metrics.description: By Vertues INTELLECTUALL, are always understood such abilityes of the mind, as men praise, value, and desire should be in themselves; and go commonly under the name of a Good Witte.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intellectual virtues are mental abilities praiseworthy in themselves (collected under 'good wit'); they are the targets for appraisal when judging minds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Natural wit (components)
rubrics_metrics.description: This NATURALL WITTE consisteth principally in two things; Celerity Of Imagining (swift succession of one thought to another) and Steddy Direction to some approved end.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Natural wit is acquired by use and experience (without formal instruction). Its defect is dulness (slowness of imagination) or lack of steadiness (distraction).

rubrics_metrics.name: Acquired wit (reason/science)
rubrics_metrics.description: As for Acquired Wit ... there is none but Reason; which is grounded on the right use of Speech; and produceth the Sciences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acquired wit arises from method and instruction (reason). It yields systematic knowledge (science) and is distinct from natural quickness of imagination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good fancy (imaginative similarity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Those that observe their similitudes ... are sayd to have a Good Wit; by which ... is meant a Good Fancy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good fancy notices rare or apt similitudes and supplies inventive illustrations and metaphors. Fancy pleases through novelty and invention but must be guided by judgement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good judgement / distinguishing
rubrics_metrics.description: They that observe their differences, and dissimilitudes ... in case such discerning be not easie, are said to have a Good Judgement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judgement discerns differences and is particularly valued in matters of conversation and business; when present, judgement is commended even if fancy is ordinary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discretion (judgement applied to time/place/person)
rubrics_metrics.description: Particularly in matter of conversation and businesse; wherein, times, places, and persons are to be discerned, this Vertue is called DISCRETION.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discretion is practical judgement — knowing what is appropriate given time, place, and company. Lack of discretion makes otherwise clever fancy seem like folly; discretion legitimizes otherwise coarse topics in professional contexts (e.g., anatomists).

rubrics_metrics.name: Fancy without judgement is not a virtue
rubrics_metrics.description: The former, that is, Fancy, without the help of Judgement, is not commended as a Vertue: but the later which is Judgement, and Discretion, is commended for it selfe, without the help of Fancy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Excessive un-directed imagination leads to digressions and loss of purpose; a great fancy without steadiness is a kind of madness. Balance is required: fancy must not displease by indiscretion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate mix of fancy and judgement by genre
rubrics_metrics.description: In a good Poem ... both Judgement and Fancy are required: But the Fancy must be more eminent ... In a good History, the Judgement must be eminent ... In Orations of Praise and Invectives, the Fancy is praedominant ... In Demonstration ... Judgement does all; except sometimes the understanding have need to be opened by some apt similitude ... For Metaphors ... are in this case utterly excluded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different literary/persuasive genres require different balances: poetry and invective privilege fancy; history and demonstration privilege judgement; metaphors are inappropriate in rigorous demonstration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prudence (practical foresight)
rubrics_metrics.description: When the thoughts of a man, that has a designe in hand, running over a multitude of things, observes how they conduce to that designe ... This wit of his is called PRUDENCE; and dependeth on much Experience, and Memory of the like things, and their consequences heretofore.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prudence is experience-based practical reasoning about how means lead to ends. Its variation among people is less than for fancy or judgement because experience of similar age tends to be comparable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Craft as corrupt prudence
rubrics_metrics.description: To Prudence, if you adde the use of unjust, or dishonest means ... you have that Crooked Wisdome, which is called CRAFT; which is a signe of Pusillanimity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Craft differs from prudence by moral character of means: employing unjust or deceitful means marks a vice; related terms: versutia (shifting), versura (usury).

rubrics_metrics.name: Passions shape differences in wit
rubrics_metrics.description: The causes of this difference of Witts, are in the Passions: and the difference of Passions, proceedeth partly from the different Constitution of the body, and partly from different Education ... The Passions that most of all cause the differences of Wit, are principally, the more or lesse Desire of Power, of Riches, of Knowledge, and of Honour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Desires (especially desire of power and its manifestations) direct the mind's attention and hence produce differing patterns of imagination and judgement across individuals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Giddiness, dulness, madness mapped to passion strength
rubrics_metrics.description: To have no Desire, is to be Dead: so to have weak Passions, is Dulnesse; and to have Passions indifferently for every thing, GIDDINESSE, and Distraction; and to have stronger, and more vehement Passions ... is that which men call MADNESSE.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hobbes maps cognitive dispositions to passion strength: weak passions → dulness; indifferent passions → giddiness/distraction; excessive passions → madness. This is diagnostic of mental states.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rage/Fury as a form of madness
rubrics_metrics.description: Pride, subjecteth a man to Anger, the excesse whereof, is the Madnesse called RAGE, and FURY.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Excessive desire for revenge, jealous love, or vehement opinion (including self-conceit) may damage organs and become raging madness; collective rage is amplified in crowds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Melancholy as madness from dejection
rubrics_metrics.description: Dejection, subjects a man to causelesse fears; which is a Madnesse commonly called MELANCHOLY ... apparent also in divers manners; as in haunting of solitudes, and graves; in superstitious behaviour; and in fearing some one, some another particular thing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Melancholy manifests as causeless fears and superstitious or solitary behaviour; it is one species within the broader genus of madness caused by passion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Insignificant speech / Absurdity (verbal madness)
rubrics_metrics.description: That abuse of words ... by the Name of Absurdity. And that is, when men speak such words, as put together, have in them no signification at all ... either through misunderstanding or intention to deceive by obscurity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typical in abstruse scholastic or theological disputes; examples: obscure technical translations that yield unintelligible propositions. This is counted among forms of madness; anti-pattern: deliberate obscurity used to deceive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two kinds of knowledge: fact and consequence
rubrics_metrics.description: There are of KNOWLEDGE two kinds; whereof one is Knowledge Of Fact: the other Knowledge Of The Consequence Of One Affirmation To Another. The former is nothing else, but Sense and Memory ... The later is called Science; and is Conditionall ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Knowledge of fact (sense & memory) is absolute and required of witnesses; knowledge of consequences (science) is conditional and required of philosophers. Distinguish epistemic aims when evaluating knowledge claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: History as register of knowledge of fact (natural vs civil)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Register of Knowledge Of Fact is called History. ... one called Naturall History ... The other, is Civill History; which is the History of the Voluntary Actions of men in Common-wealths.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Natural history records facts of nature independent of human will (metals, plants, animals); civil history records voluntary human actions and political events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Science (philosophy) as demonstration of consequences and its taxonomy
rubrics_metrics.description: Science, that is, Knowledge of Consequences; which is called also PHILOSOPHY ... (followed by a hierarchical table: philosophia prima, geometry, arithmetique, astronomy, geography, mechanics, engineers, architecture, navigation, meteorology, scioography, astrology, physics of terrestrial bodies, optics, musique, ethique, poetry, rhetorique, logique, justice, and politiques).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sciences are books containing demonstrations of consequences. Hobbes provides an explicit taxonomy subdividing natural philosophy (principia, mathematica, mechanics, astronomy, meteorology, optics, music), qualities of animals and men (ethics, poetry, rhetoric, logic), and political/civil philosophy. Use this taxonomy to classify kinds of inquiry and their proper methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power defined and its sources
rubrics_metrics.description: The POWER of a Man ... is his present means, to obtain some future apparent Good. And is either Originall, or Instrumentall. Naturall Power ... Instrumentall are those Powers, which acquired by these, or by fortune, are means and Instruments to acquire more: as Riches, Reputation, Friends, and the Secret working of God, which men call Good Luck.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Power increases when combined and compounds like motion: natural faculties (strength, prudence, eloquence, form) and instrumental means (riches, friends, reputation) both supply power. Reputation of power counts as power because it attracts adhesion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Worth as price determined by others' needs/judgement
rubrics_metrics.description: The Value, or WORTH of a man, is as of all other things, his Price; that is to say, so much as would be given for the use of his Power: and therefore is not absolute; but a thing dependant on the need and judgement of another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A person's worth varies by context (an able military leader is high value in war but less in peace). Buyers, not sellers, determine price. Honour and dishonour are public manifestations of valuation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dignity as public worth allocated by commonwealth
rubrics_metrics.description: The publique worth of a man, which is the Value set on him by the Common-wealth, is that which men commonly call DIGNITY. And this Value of him by the Common-wealth, is understood, by offices of Command, Judicature, publike Employment; or by Names and Titles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dignity is institutional/public recognition (offices, titles, employment). It signals the commonwealth's opinion of a person's value and confers social power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Actions and signs that honour or dishonour
rubrics_metrics.description: To pray to another, for ayde ... is to HONOUR; To obey, is to Honour; To give great gifts ... is to Honour; To give little gifts, is to Dishonour; To shew any signe of love, or feare of another, is to Honour; To contemne, or lesse to love or feare then he expects, is to Dishonour ... To employ in counsell, or in actions of difficulty, is to Honour; To deny employment ... is to Dishonour ... To praise ... is to Honour; To revile, mock, or pitty, is to Dishonour ... To imitate, is to Honour; To imitate ones Enemy, is to Dishonour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A long list of social behaviours function as markers: prayer/appeal, obedience, gifts, deference, praise, attention, employment, imitation, trust, and agreement are honouring acts; neglect, insult, distrust, disdain, refusal, and imitation of enemies are dishonouring. These acts are natural signs of attributing power to another and are context-sensitive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sovereign-created honours (civil honours)
rubrics_metrics.description: A Soveraigne doth Honour a Subject, with whatsoever Title, or Office, or Employment, or Action, that he himselfe will have taken for a signe of his will to Honour him.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In commonwealths, sovereigns can institute arbitrary signs of honour (titles, ceremonies). Public honours can be created by authority and thereby become recognized signs of power.

rubrics_metrics.name: What counts as honourable or dishonourable possessions/actions
rubrics_metrics.description: Honourable is whatsoever possession, action, or quality, is an argument and signe of Power. And therefore To be Honoured, loved, or feared of many, is Honourable; ... Good fortune (if lasting,) Honourable; Ill fortune, and losses, Dishonourable. Riches, are Honourable; Poverty, Dishonourable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Honour attaches to attributes that signal power: popularity, sustained good fortune, riches. Losses or poverty reduce honour. The criterion is instrumental (does the possession/action signal power?), not moral.
